So I recently booked a domestic flight on United.com via Kayak. Before completing my booking, I saw an option to upgrade (which I'm willing to pay for, if the price is right): over $700 each way. That's too rich for my blood, so I decline.

Then after booking, I get prompted to upgrade again: this time for just $150. Same upgrade, a fraction of the price, and just seconds later.

Curious stuff. I've seen the $150 upgrade at the time of check-in, but never months in advance. Upon choosing my First Class seat, I see that the entire First cabin is empty.

So United was being sneaky: They wanted to see if I would pay the full $700 to upgrade, but after I declined and committed to economy, they gave me the real price of an upgrade.

There is no "real" price, and they simply want to charge the most that someone is willing to pay. One the one hand it feels bad, but on the other it's very economically efficient. Imagine the following situation. There are two clients: the price-insensitive expense-account traveler and the casual /u/RunsWithScissors. Then consider three possible pricing modes: upgrade costs $700 only, upgrade costs $150 only, upgrade costs varies depending on booking time.

In case one: Business traveler pays $700, you pay $0 (extra that is, you've booked the base fare) = $700 extra for the airline.

In case two: Business traveler pays $150, you pay $150 = $300 extra for the airline.

And then the variable-pricing case three: Business traveler pays $700, you pay $150 = $850 for the airline. Clearly the best deal for them and for you, and the other guy doesn't care anyway, so he's happy too.

Yeah, I get it. It's price discrimination. If someone only wants to book a trip if they get first class, you can charge them more.

Still... Haven't seen that behavior before. Makes me glad I booked directly on the airline's website, because I wouldn't have seen that offer with a booking site.
